newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Fyffes says business flat, warns on profit.
newsitem.headline: Fyffes says business flat, warns on profit.

text.p: Irish fruit and vegetable distributor Fyffes Plc said on Monday that profits at the half-way stage may be down on last year.
"Business has been flatter than expected in the early months of 1997," Fyffes said in a statement.
It said as a result profits at the half-way stage may be slightly down on last year.
Fyffes said this was due to a price deflation across its product range allied to recent unfavourable currency trends.
"Current trading has improved and while it is too early to predict the outcome for the full year, we are hopeful of better trading in the second half," Fyffes said.
Deputy chairman Carl McCann said the announcement was a cautionary note rather than a profit warning.
"What we're seeing at the moment is a flatter first half and it's possible profits may be a bit behind last year," he told reporters after the group's annual meeting.

McCann said currency factors had affected the company in two ways. The strength of the Irish pound against the continental European currencies was affecting the translation of Fyffes' European profits into Irish pounds while much of the company's costs are in dollars and the U.S. currency has performed very strongly this year.
Fyffes is also facing price deflation right across the board with prices down by an average of 10 percent.
"But it's a six-month issue and hopefully it will remain a six-month issue," McCann said.
The group is currently in active discussions with a number of parties in Europe on acquisition opportunities but McCann said no deals were imminent.

McCann also said Fyffes would be inclined to look "more seriously" at a share buyback following recent changes introduced in the 1997 Irish Finance Bill which allow a company to buy back shares without advance corporation tax liability.
"It's the first time we have had a clear road forward. But what you have to weigh up is do you have a big enough deal coming down the road or do you buy back shares?" he said.
